content: A small subset of individuals infected with COVID-19 develop severe disease, which is characterized by significant inflammation, microvascular damage, and coagulopathy. These pathological processes can result in myocardial injury, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and arterial occlusive events. Individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease are at an elevated risk of experiencing these complications. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the prevalence of pre-existing cardiovascular comorbidities in individuals with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 across various settings, including the community, care homes, and hospitals. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the nature and frequency of cardiovascular complications and clinical events that occur in these patients. An electronic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, covid-19.cochrane.org, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the EU Clinical Trial Register. The search covered studies published from December 2019 to July 24, 2020. The review included prospective and retrospective cohort studies, controlled before-and-after studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Controlled trials were analyzed as cohort studies, irrespective of treatment allocation. Only peer-reviewed studies with at least 100 participants were included, and studies published in languages other than English or only available on pre-print servers were excluded. Two independent reviewers screened the search results and extracted data. Due to significant variability in study designs, reported outcomes, and outcome metrics, a narrative synthesis of the data was performed instead of a meta-analysis. All included studies were critically appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist for prevalence studies and the JBI checklist for case series. A total of 220 studies were included in the review. The majority of these studies originated from China (47.7%) and the USA (20.9%), with 9.5% from Italy. Most studies were retrospective in design (89.5%), while three studies (1.4%) were RCTs, and 20 studies (9.1%) were prospective. Using the JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies, 75 studies achieved a full score of 9, 57 studies scored 8, 31 studies scored 7, five studies scored 6, three studies scored 5, and one study scored 3. For case series, 30 studies received a full score of 10, six studies scored 9, 11 studies scored 8, and one study scored 5. The review found that hypertension (reported in 189 studies, with a total of 174,414 participants; weighted mean prevalence [WMP]: 36.1%), diabetes (reported in 197 studies, with a total of 569,188 participants; WMP: 22.1%), and ischemic heart disease (reported in 94 studies, with a total of 100,765 participants; WMP: 10.5%) were highly prevalent among individuals hospitalized with COVID-19. These conditions were associated with an increased risk of mortality. Among hospitalized patients, biomarkers indicative of cardiac stress or injury were frequently abnormal. The incidence of cardiovascular complications was substantial, with arrhythmias reported in 22 studies (13,115 participants; weighted mean incidence [WMI]: 9.3%), heart failure in 20 studies (29,317 participants; WMI: 6.8%), and thrombotic complications such as VTE in 16 studies (7,700 participants; WMI: 7.4%). In conclusion, this systematic review highlights that cardiometabolic comorbidities are common among individuals hospitalized with COVID-19, and cardiovascular complications are frequently observed in this population. The authors plan to update this review and conduct a formal meta-analysis using a more homogeneous subset of high-certainty studies.
